stem: A company runs virtual machines on a public cloud provider's IaaS platform. Who is responsible for applying operating system security patches to those VMs?

options.text: The customer
options.why: Under IaaS the provider supplies compute, storage and network. Everything from the guest operating system upward belongs to the customer.

options.text: The cloud provider
options.why: The provider patches the hypervisor and the physical infrastructure. The guest OS inside your VM is yours.

options.text: Shared equally between both parties
options.why: The matrix assigns each layer to one party. It does not split a single layer.

options.text: Whichever party the contract names, with no default
options.why: The service model sets the default division, which is precisely what the responsibility matrix documents.

stem: Customer records stored in a SaaS CRM were exposed because a sharing permission was set to 'anyone with the link'. Who is responsible?

options.text: The customer, because configuration and access are never transferred to the provider
options.why: Data, identity and configuration remain the customer's responsibility in every service model, SaaS included.

options.text: The provider, because in SaaS they manage the entire stack
options.why: They manage the application, the runtime and the infrastructure. They do not choose your sharing settings.

options.text: The provider, because the exposure was through their application's feature
options.why: The feature worked as designed. The customer configured it to share publicly.

options.text: Neither, since no system was breached
options.why: A data exposure is a security incident whether or not anything was technically compromised.

stem: Which statement correctly compares containers with virtual machines?

options.text: Containers share the host kernel, which makes them lighter and their isolation weaker
options.why: The shared kernel explains both the millisecond startup and the fact that a kernel flaw affects every container on the host.

options.text: Containers each run a full guest operating system, like a lightweight VM
options.why: That is what a virtual machine does. A container packages only the application and its dependencies.

options.text: Containers provide stronger isolation than virtual machines because of their smaller attack surface
options.why: The image is smaller and the isolation boundary is weaker, because the kernel is shared rather than virtualised.

options.text: Containers require a hypervisor, virtual machines do not
options.why: Reversed. Virtual machines run on a hypervisor; containers run on a container runtime over the shared kernel.

stem: An attacker breaks out of a guest virtual machine and executes code on the hypervisor. What is this called, and why does it matter so much?

options.text: VM escape, because it exposes every other guest on that host
options.why: The hypervisor is the isolation boundary for all guests. Compromising it collapses the separation between every tenant on the machine.

options.text: Resource reuse, because memory is shared between guests
options.why: Resource reuse is when data lingers in memory or storage reallocated to another tenant. That is a leak, not a breakout.

options.text: Container escape, because the kernel is shared
options.why: Container escape breaks out to a shared host kernel. Virtual machines do not share a kernel.

options.text: Privilege escalation, confined to the affected guest
options.why: The defining feature is that it is not confined to the guest. It reaches the host.

stem: An engineering team states that their SCADA network is air gapped. An audit finds a single firewalled link to the corporate network used for historian data. How should this be assessed?

options.text: It is not air gapped; it is logically segmented and should be described and defended as such
options.why: An air gap means no connection exists. One firewalled link is a controlled path, and treating it as an air gap leads to weaker controls than a connected network requires.

options.text: It remains air gapped, because the link is firewalled
options.why: A firewall filters a connection. It does not remove one.

options.text: It is physically isolated, since the SCADA hardware is separate
options.why: Separate hardware with a network link between them is not isolation.

options.text: It is microsegmented
options.why: Microsegmentation applies policy per workload. One perimeter link between two networks is not that.

stem: A genuinely air gapped system was infected with malware. What is the most likely vector?

options.text: Removable media carried across the gap
options.why: With no network path, data still has to move somehow, and USB media is the classic route into an air gapped environment.

options.text: A phishing email opened by an operator
options.why: An air gapped system has no mail connectivity, which is what the gap means.

options.text: Exploitation of an internet facing service
options.why: There is no internet facing service. If there were, it would not be air gapped.

options.text: A compromised VPN credential
options.why: A VPN is a network path, which an air gapped system by definition does not have.

stem: An organisation defines its entire cloud environment in version controlled templates that are applied automatically. What is the main security benefit?

options.text: Configuration is consistent, reviewable and reproducible, so drift and one-off mistakes are reduced
options.why: Infrastructure as code makes the environment auditable and repeatable, and changes go through review like any other code.

options.text: The cloud provider becomes responsible for the resulting configuration
options.why: Configuration is the customer's responsibility in every service model. Automating it does not transfer it.

options.text: It removes the need to patch the resulting systems
options.why: It makes rebuilding patched systems easier. It does not remove the requirement.

options.text: It provides isolation equivalent to an air gap
options.why: IaC describes how infrastructure is defined. It says nothing about network separation.

stem: In a SCADA environment controlling a water treatment process, how do the usual security priorities change?

options.text: Availability and safety come first, because an outage is a physical consequence rather than an inconvenience
options.why: Operational technology inverts the familiar ordering. A control system that stops can mean a process out of control, so measures that risk availability are weighed very differently.

options.text: Confidentiality comes first, because process data is highly sensitive
options.why: Setpoints and sensor readings are rarely the crown jewels. Keeping the process running safely is.

options.text: The priorities are identical to corporate IT
options.why: They are not, which is why these systems are treated separately.

options.text: Integrity is irrelevant because the data is only telemetry
options.why: Integrity is critical: falsified readings cause operators or logic to act wrongly on a physical process.

stem: A proposal is made to install an endpoint detection agent on controllers running a real-time operating system. Why is this likely to be rejected?

options.text: A real-time system guarantees deterministic timing; an agent consuming unpredictable CPU can cause the system to miss deadlines, which is a functional failure
options.why: Determinism is a requirement, not a preference. Added latency is a fault in a way it never is on a general-purpose host, which is why these systems are protected from the network instead.

options.text: Real-time systems have no network connectivity to monitor
options.why: Many are networked, which is precisely why they need protecting.

options.text: Endpoint agents cannot detect threats on embedded platforms
options.why: The obstacle is the effect on timing and the usual absence of a supported build, not detection capability in principle.

options.text: The agent would violate the vendor's data protection obligations
options.why: Vendor certification is an obstacle for different reasons: changing the configuration can void support.

stem: What architectural characteristic do IoT devices, embedded systems and industrial controllers most commonly share that shapes how they must be secured?

options.text: Limited or absent update mechanisms and very long service lives, so they outlive vendor support
options.why: A controller installed for twenty years will spend most of that unsupported. The design has to assume the device will not be fixed, which pushes everything onto network controls.

options.text: They all run full general-purpose operating systems
options.why: Most run minimal or real-time systems with no capacity for conventional tooling.

options.text: They are always air gapped
options.why: Rarely true in practice, and assuming it is the reason many of these environments are reachable.

options.text: They hold little data, so compromise has limited impact
options.why: Impact is physical: they control processes. The data they hold is not the measure.

stem: An organisation consolidates security management of forty offices into one central platform. What does it gain, and what does it accept?

options.text: Consistent policy and a single view, at the cost of a larger blast radius if the centre is compromised or unavailable
options.why: Centralisation concentrates control and consequence together. The trade is real in both directions, which is why the useful question is what was accepted rather than which is better.

options.text: Both better consistency and better resilience, with no meaningful trade-off
options.why: Resilience generally worsens: the centre becomes a single point of failure for all forty sites.

options.text: Better resilience at the cost of consistency
options.why: Reversed. Consistency is what centralisation buys.

options.text: Lower cost with no change to the security posture
options.why: The posture changes substantially in both directions, whatever happens to cost.

stem: A team must stand up a new service in three weeks with minimal capital expenditure, accepting higher running costs later. Which architectural property is being prioritised?

options.text: Ease of deployment, traded against long-run operating cost
options.why: Speed to stand up is being bought, and the stem states the price: higher ongoing cost. That is the shape of every architecture trade-off question.

options.text: Ease of recovery
options.why: That concerns how quickly you restore after failure, which the stem does not mention.

options.text: Responsiveness
options.why: Latency to the user, which is also not in the stem.

options.text: Risk transference
options.why: Moving risk to a provider may be a side effect, and the stated requirement is time and capital.

stem: Two designs are compared. A: stateless containers rebuilt from images in minutes. B: a long-lived stateful server restored from backup over several hours. Which property distinguishes them, and why does it matter for security?

options.text: Ease of recovery; a design you can rebuild quickly makes reimaging after compromise cheap, so the secure response stops being the expensive one
options.why: Recovery cost shapes behaviour. When rebuilding takes minutes, nobody argues for cleaning a compromised host in place.

options.text: Scalability, since containers scale more easily
options.why: True and not what the stem contrasts, which is restoration time.

options.text: Responsiveness, since containers start faster
options.why: Responsiveness is latency in serving requests, not time to restore.

options.text: Cost, since containers are cheaper to run
options.why: Not stated, and not the distinction being drawn.

stem: A company moves its payroll system to a managed SaaS provider, citing risk transference. A breach later exposes employee records. What has actually transferred?

options.text: Operational responsibility and some financial consequence; the accountability to employees and regulators remains with the company
options.why: You can contract away work and some liability. The obligation to notify, and the reputational and regulatory exposure, stay where the data subjects' relationship is.

options.text: Full accountability, since the provider now controls the system
options.why: Accountability cannot be purchased away. The company remains the controller of its employees' data.

options.text: Nothing: risk transference is not possible in cloud arrangements
options.why: Overcorrection. Real operational risk and contractual liability do move.

options.text: Only the cost of running the system
options.why: Genuine operational risk transfers too, which is a legitimate reason to do it.

stem: Which TWO statements about specialised and distributed architectures are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: In operational technology, availability and safety typically outrank confidentiality
options.why: An outage in a physical process is a safety event, which reorders the usual priorities.

options.text: Centralising management concentrates both control and the consequences of failure
options.why: The same property that delivers consistency makes the centre a single point of failure.

options.text: Endpoint agents are the primary control for real-time controllers
options.why: They threaten the timing guarantees these systems exist to provide; network isolation is the usual answer.

options.text: Decentralised architectures are inherently more secure
options.why: They contain failures better and drift more. Neither is inherently more secure.

options.text: Moving to a managed service transfers accountability for a breach
options.why: Responsibility and some liability move; accountability to regulators and data subjects does not.

stem: A retailer lets each of its 200 stores manage its own firewall rules locally. Which outcome should the security team expect?

options.text: A compromise at one store tends to stay at that store, but rules drift apart and the central team loses visibility
options.why: Decentralising buys containment and pays in consistency and visibility. Both halves of that trade show up here.

options.text: Consistency improves, because each store knows its own needs best
options.why: Two hundred independent rule sets drift by default. Consistency is what centralisation buys, and it has been given up.

options.text: The blast radius of a single compromise grows
options.why: Blast radius grows when control is concentrated. Here a compromised store's firewall reaches only that store.

options.text: Visibility improves, because more administrators are watching
options.why: Each administrator sees one store. Nobody sees the whole picture, which is the visibility gap decentralisation creates.
